target_customer: Growers of drip-irrigated specialty crops such as tree nuts and vineyards in California
problem: Farmers lacked a field-scale measure of actual crop water use, so irrigation decisions relied on estimates or single-plant and soil probes.
business_model: Hardware sensor kept by the company with a per-sensor per-season data subscription (reported at $1,500 per sensor per season)

founders.name: Tom Shapland
education: UC Davis, master's and PhD in Horticulture and Agronomy Graduate Group, graduated 2012
founders.background_notes: Atmospheric science background per TechCrunch; licensed the UC Davis sensor technology.

founders.name: Jeff LaBarge
founders.background_notes: Software engineer per press; no further background found.

technical_complexity.rationale: Combined a UC Davis licensed above-canopy evapotranspiration measurement with field hardware, cellular transmission and servers, which is hardware plus agronomy science for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Exclusive UC Davis license for the sensor system gave a technology moat, while the founder said alternatives were costly, single-plant or only estimates. Hardware and data could accumulate across seasons.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied it in the years sourced; CropX acquired the company in January 2023 to enter drip-irrigated specialty crops.

market_need_then: California drought in 2014 to 2015 raised the stakes on water use, and the founder said existing tools were too costly outside the lab, covered one plant, or gave only estimates (UC Davis article, March 2015).

branding.domain_note: Used tuletechnologies.com; it now redirects to a CropX transition page.

identity.voice_and_tone: Plain agronomy language aimed at growers: one number for the irrigation decision.

brand_strength.rationale: Searches found coverage of the product but no press about the brand itself, no mascot or community; niche recognition among growers only.

outcome_analysis: Tule commercialized a UC Davis licensed evapotranspiration sensor during the California drought, raised a seed of reportedly over $1 million from Khosla and Bloomberg Beta in 2015, and stayed a small specialty-crop business before CropX acquired it in January 2023 with undisclosed terms and all staff joining. The exit looks like a modest strategic sale rather than a large outcome. The pivot date for Tule Vision is not sourced.
notes: Databases list about $120K total, which matches the YC amount only. The seed amount of over $1 million comes from TechCrunch and the UC Davis article, both stating it loosely. Neither source names competitors, so the list is empty. Company site redirects to CropX. Tule Vision phone photo product was added later; date not sourced, so no pivot recorded.
